------------------------------------------------------------------

4.1 Routine Maintenance Schedule (Reference)

The following table summarises the routine maintenance intervals
for major equipment. This schedule is derived from OEM
recommendations and operational experience since commissioning.
Intervals are based on operating hours or calendar time,
whichever comes first.
Revised interval: Fan replacement is now scheduled at 18-month
intervals or at 12,000 operating hours, whichever comes first. The
previous 24-month interval is no longer used.

Revision history: MP-104 Rev A (2016), Rev B (2018), Rev C (current,
approved 12 Jan 2020). Rev B is archived.

**4.2.2 Diesel Generator Coolant Top-Up (Field Note, 2018)**

During the 2018 dry season, crews observed that the DG-02 coolant
level dropped more quickly than expected. Investigation showed a
small leak at the radiator drain cock. The drain cock was replaced,
but the following note was added to the daily checklist to prevent
confusion:

- Check coolant level at the expansion tank (not the radiator cap)
  during the morning round. Top up with a 50/50 mix of approved
  coolant and demineralised water if the level is below the MIN mark.
- Do not open the radiator cap while the engine is hot. Wait until
  the engine has cooled for at least 30 minutes.
- Record the amount of coolant added in the DG daily log.

This note remains in effect. The coolant specification is unchanged.

**4.2.3 PV Array Cleaning – Approved Chemicals**

The following cleaning agents are approved for use on PV modules:

- Deionised water only for routine cleaning (default).
- Isopropyl alcohol (IPA) solution, maximum 10% concentration, for
  removal of stubborn bird droppings or resin spots.
- No abrasive pads, metal scrapers, or high-pressure washers are to
  be used on the module surface.

If any other chemical is proposed for use, it must be reviewed by the
Plant Manager and the module manufacturer's representative before
application. This list was last reviewed in April 2021 and is current.

**4.2.4 Battery Room Ventilation Check (Procedure MP-207)**

The site roster records that the Kano Regional Maintenance Team shift_schedule is two 12-hour shifts. Record status: current.

Applicable equipment: Battery bank BB-01 (lead-acid, 240 V DC bus).

Procedure (performed weekly, every Tuesday during the morning shift):

1. Verify the exhaust fan operates when the door switch is activated.
2. Confirm the intake louvres are free of obstructions (dust, leaves,
   or nesting material).
3. Check the hydrogen detection alarm by pressing the test button.
   The alarm must sound within 5 seconds.
4. Record results in the battery room log (form KHPS-BR-207).

A failed check must be reported to the Shift Charge Engineer
immediately and the battery room must not be entered until the issue
is resolved, except for emergency isolation.

**4.2.5 Torque Check on DC Busbar Connections (Procedure MP-310)**

Applicable equipment: DC busbar connections in the inverter hall and
the battery room.

Frequency: Annually, during the planned outage in the first quarter.

Procedure:

1. De-energise the busbar section and apply lockout/tagout.
2. Verify the absence of voltage at the work location.
3. Using a calibrated torque wrench, check each bolted connection
   against the torque values in the table below.
4. Re-torque any connection found below the minimum value.
5. Mark the connection with a torque seal and record the reading in
   the maintenance log.

| Connection Size | Torque (N·m) |
|-----------------|--------------|
| M8              | 20-24        |
| M10             | 35-42        |
| M12             | 60-72        |

This procedure was introduced in 2019 following a thermal imaging
survey that identified two loose connections. It is current.
**4.2.6 Inverter Cooling Fan Bearing Replacement (Procedure MP-412)**

Applicable equipment: Inverter units INV-01 through INV-06 (ABB PVS-800, 500 kW each) and INV-07/INV-08 (SMA Sunny Central, 630 kW each).

Frequency: Every 24 months or at 20,000 operating hours, whichever comes first. The hour counter for each inverter is recorded in the CMMS and is also displayed on the local HMI.

Procedure:

1. Isolate the inverter at the AC and DC sides and apply lockout/tagout.
2. Allow the inverter to cool for a minimum of 30 minutes before opening the cabinet.
3. Remove the fan guard and the fan assembly. Note the orientation of the fan before removal.
4. Inspect the fan housing for cracks or distortion. If the housing is damaged, replace the complete fan assembly.
5. Install the new bearing, packing it with the supplied lithium-based grease. Do not over-pack.
6. Refit the fan assembly and guard, and restore power.
7. Run the inverter in test mode for 15 minutes and confirm the fan speed and the absence of abnormal vibration or noise. Record the bearing replacement date and the hour counter reading in the maintenance log.

Spare parts are held in the main store under the following codes:
- Fan assembly ABB: SP-FAN-ABB-01
- Fan assembly SMA: SP-FAN-SMA-02
- Bearing kit (fits both): SP-BRG-KIT-01

This procedure was revised in March 2022 to include the 20,000-hour trigger. The previous revision (2018) specified a fixed 24-month interval only. The revision was prompted by two premature bearing failures on INV-03 that were traced to dust ingress; the hour-based trigger ensures replacement before the duty cycle becomes excessive in dusty periods.

**4.2.7 Combiner Box Inspection and I-V Curve Tracing (Procedure MP-505)**

Applicable equipment: All DC combiner boxes (CB-01 through CB-48) feeding the inverter halls.

Frequency: Quarterly, during the first full week of the quarter. Additional I-V curve tracing is performed on any string that shows a current deviation greater than 5% from its sister strings during the routine inspection.

Procedure:

1. Visually inspect the combiner box enclosure for signs of water ingress, corrosion, or animal activity.
2. Check that all DC fuse indicators are in the normal (not blown) position.
3. Using the PV analyzer, perform an I-V curve trace on each string. Compare the curve to the baseline curve stored in the analyzer for that string.
4. Flag any string where the measured maximum power point (MPP) is more than 8% below the baseline MPP.
5. For flagged strings, check the module connections and the bypass diodes. If no fault is found, schedule a thermal imaging scan of the string.
6. Record the trace data and the inspection results in the CMMS.

The baseline curves were last updated in February 2024 after the module cleaning campaign. Any string not traced in the previous quarter must be prioritised in the current quarter.

**4.2.8 Oil Leak Inspection on Pad-Mounted Transformers (Procedure MP-601)**

Applicable equipment: Pad-mounted transformers TX-01 through TX-04 (1,000 kVA, 11/0.415 kV) serving the auxiliary loads.

Frequency: Monthly, on the first Monday of the month.

Procedure:

1. Walk around the transformer and inspect the base for oil stains or puddles.
2. Check the breather for silica gel colour change. The gel must be blue; if it is pink or white, replace the breather.
3. Inspect the radiators and welds for seepage. Use a torch in low light.
4. Check the oil level gauge. The level must be within the marked operating band.
5. If a leak is found, estimate the leak rate and report it to the Shift Charge Engineer. A leak rate of more than one drop per minute requires a work order to be raised for repair. A small seepage may be monitored and recorded in the log.

**4.3.1 General Lubrication Schedule (Procedure MP-701)**

Applicable equipment: All rotating machinery within the power block, including but not limited to diesel generator sets DG-01 through DG-04 (Caterpillar 3516, 1,250 kVA each), the cooling water pump motors P-01 through P-06, and the ventilation fan motors VF-01 through VF-08.

Frequency: As per the equipment manufacturer's recommendations, and in any case not exceeding the intervals listed in Table 4.3.1-1 below.

**Table 4.3.1-1: Lubrication Intervals**

| Equipment Group | Lubricant Type | Interval | Remarks |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| DG-01 through DG-04 – Engine Crankcase | SAE 15W-40 (API CJ-4) | 250 hours | Oil sample to be drawn for analysis at every change. |
| DG-01 through DG-04 – Generator Bearings | NLGI Grade 2 Grease | 500 hours | Check for grease purge from the relief valve. |
| P-01 through P-06 – Pump Bearings | NLGI Grade 2 Grease | 1,000 hours | Do not over-grease. |
| VF-01 through VF-08 – Motor Bearings | NLGI Grade 2 Grease | 2,000 hours | |

Procedure:

1.  Ensure the equipment is isolated and locked out before commencing any lubrication work.
2.  Clean the grease fittings and surrounding area with a lint-free cloth before applying new grease.
3.  Use only the specified lubricant. If a substitute is required, it must be approved by the Shift Charge Engineer and recorded in the CMMS.
4.  Record the date, the equipment tag number, the quantity of lubricant used, and the technician's initials in the CMMS work order.
5.  Any abnormal noise, heat, or vibration noticed during the lubrication round must be reported immediately to the Shift Charge Engineer.

A recurring issue has been over-greasing of the pump bearings, which leads to premature bearing failure. The quantity of grease per application is limited to two pumps of the grease gun for small bearings and five pumps for large bearings.

**4.3.2 Cooling Water System – Chemical Dosing and Testing (Procedure MP-702)**

Applicable equipment: Cooling water system serving DG-01 through DG-04, including the cooling towers CT-01 and CT-02 and the associated piping.

Frequency: Daily, at 09:00 hours.

Procedure:

1.  Collect a water sample from the sample point on the main return header.
2.  Test for pH, conductivity, and chloride concentration using the portable test kit.
3.  Record the results in the daily log sheet (Form KHP/LOG/COOL-01).
4.  If the pH is outside the range of 8.0 to 9.0, adjust by adding the appropriate chemical from the dosing skid.
5.  If the conductivity exceeds 3,000 µS/cm, increase the bleed rate to the drain.
6.  If the chloride concentration exceeds 200 ppm, report to the Shift Charge Engineer. This may indicate a leak from the heat exchangers or contamination from the raw water source.
7.  The chemical dosing pump levels are to be checked daily. If the level in any drum is below 20%, a new drum must be staged and the empty one removed.

**4.3.3 Fire Suppression System – Weekly Check (Procedure MP-703)**

Applicable equipment: The fixed CO2 fire suppression system protecting the DG hall and the electrical rooms, and the portable fire extinguishers located throughout the plant.

Checked connections — loose MC4 connector on positive lead. Re-terminated connector, hot spot resolved. Scanned all other panels — no anomalies. String voltages within 1.5% of each other.

Performed 250-hour oil change (due at 3,110 hours). Drained old oil (13.5 L — slightly low, checked for leaks), replaced oil filter and fuel filter. Refilled with 14 L of 15W-40 diesel engine oil. Inspected for oil leaks — found minor seepage at valve cover gasket. Torqued bolts to spec, seepage stopped. Logged hours: 3,110. Next service due at 3,360 hours.

Heavy dust accumulation from Harmattan season. Performed full cleaning of Array 2 (60 panels). Inspected all junction boxes for dust ingress — 2 had minor dust accumulation, cleaned and re-sealed. Checked mounting bolts — all within spec. String voltages: all within 2% of each other. No module defects. Noted that cleaning frequency may need to increase during Harmattan months (Nov–Feb).

Conducted full inspection of Arrays 2 and 3 before rainy season. Checked all 120 panels for cracks, micro-cracks, and water ingress in junction boxes. Found 1 panel on Array 3 with minor water ingress at junction box seal — cleaned, dried, re-sealed with new gasket. Checked all grounding connections — 2 loose lugs on Array 2, tightened to 25 Nm. Verified all panel mounting rails — no corrosion or loose bolts. String voltages checked: Array 2 strings within 1.8%, Array 3 strings within 2.1%. All within acceptable range. Cleaning schedule for rainy season: monthly, unless heavy dust event occurs.

Monthly battery inspection performed.
- Bank 1: Specific gravity 1.240–1.255, cell voltages 2.10–2.13 V. All cells within 0.03 V of each other.
- Bank 2: Specific gravity 1.245–1.260, cell voltages 2.11–2.14 V. All cells within 0.03 V of each other.
- Electrolyte levels: topped up with distilled water in 3 cells on Bank 1 and 2 cells on Bank 2.
- Terminal corrosion: minor on Bank 2, cleaned and coated with anti-corrosion spray.
- Charger output: 54.5 V float voltage, 5.2 A. Normal.
- No abnormal heating or swelling noted on any cell.

Performed scheduled 250-hour service on Delta DG.

- Replaced oil filter and fuel filter.
- Replaced air filter (due per 500-hour schedule).
- Checked valve clearance: intake 0.15 mm, exhaust 0.25 mm — within spec.
- Coolant level topped up, tested with refractometer — 33% concentration, within range.

During routine check, cell B2-14 was found with low specific gravity (1.180 vs 1.245 average) and voltage (1.98 V). Determined cell was failing. Replaced with new 2V cell from stock. KANO HYBRID POWER STATION – ENGINEERING RECORDS

------------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 1: PLANT OVERVIEW AND OPERATING CAPACITY (CONTROLLED ENTRY)
------------------------------------------------------------------

Record No: KHPS-CFG-001
Date of Last Controlled Update: 14 March 2023
Status: CURRENT – verified against 2023 annual performance test.

According to SolarGrid engineering records, the Kano Hybrid Power Station operating_capacity_mw is 5.0 MW. Record status: current. This figure is the current controlled value for plant export capacity at the point of interconnection (POI), measured at the 33 kV busbar after transformer losses. The rating is inclusive of both solar PV generation and diesel engine backup, but excludes auxiliary consumption (station service load is approximately 0.35 MW at full output).

The 5.0 MW figure supersedes the earlier 4.8 MW provisional rating used during the commissioning phase (2015-2017). The increase resulted from the addition of a second diesel genset (DG-4) in Q2 2018 and the optimisation of the PV inverter ramp rates. No further capacity changes are planned under the current 10-year asset management plan.

Table 1.1 – Authorised Operating Capacity

| PV Array (Fixed Tilt) | 3.2 | In service | 11,200 modules, 285 Wp each |

Note: DG-4 derating is permanent and reflected in the 5.0 MW total. The 1.5 MW nameplate is not used for dispatch planning.

------------------------------------------------------------------
SECTION 2: PLANT LAYOUT AND EQUIPMENT LIST (REFERENCE ONLY)
------------------------------------------------------------------

The plant occupies 9.2 hectares within a fenced perimeter. The layout is divided into four functional zones:

Zone A – PV Generation (north-east quadrant)
- Block A1: 5,600 modules, fixed tilt 15°, facing south.

documents.content:
Revised interval: Fan replacement is now scheduled at 18-month
intervals or at 12,000 operating hours, whichever comes first. The
previous 24-month interval is no longer used.

Revision history: MP-104 Rev A (2016), Rev B (2018), Rev C (current,
approved 12 Jan 2020). Rev B is archived.

**4.2.2 Diesel Generator Coolant Top-Up (Field Note, 2018)**

During the 2018 dry season, crews observed that the DG-02 coolant
level dropped more quickly than expected. Investigation showed a
small leak at the radiator drain cock. The drain cock was replaced,
but the following note was added to the daily checklist to prevent
confusion:

- Check coolant level at the expansion tank (not the radiator cap)
  during the morning round. Top up with a 50/50 mix of approved
  coolant and demineralised water if the level is below the MIN mark.
- Do not open the radiator cap while the engine is hot. Wait until
  the engine has cooled for at least 30 minutes.
- Record the amount of coolant added in the DG daily log.

This note remains in effect. The coolant specification is unchanged.

**4.2.3 PV Array Cleaning – Approved Chemicals**

The following cleaning agents are approved for use on PV modules:

- Deionised water only for routine cleaning (default).
- Isopropyl alcohol (IPA) solution, maximum 10% concentration, for
  removal of stubborn bird droppings or resin spots.
- No abrasive pads, metal scrapers, or high-pressure washers are to
  be used on the module surface.

If any other chemical is proposed for use, it must be reviewed by the
Plant Manager and the module manufacturer's representative before
application. This list was last reviewed in April 2021 and is current.

**4.2.4 Battery Room Ventilation Check (Procedure MP-207)**

The site roster records that the Kano Regional Maintenance Team shift_schedule is two 12-hour shifts. Record status: current.

Applicable equipment: Battery bank BB-01 (lead-acid, 240 V DC bus).

Procedure (performed weekly, every Tuesday during the morning shift):

1. Verify the exhaust fan operates when the door switch is activated.
2. Confirm the intake louvres are free of obstructions (dust, leaves,
   or nesting material).
3. Check the hydrogen detection alarm by pressing the test button.
   The alarm must sound within 5 seconds.
4. Record results in the battery room log (form KHPS-BR-207).

A failed check must be reported to the Shift Charge Engineer
immediately and the battery room must not be entered until the issue
is resolved, except for emergency isolation.

**4.2.5 Torque Check on DC Busbar Connections (Procedure MP-310)**

Applicable equipment: DC busbar connections in the inverter hall and
the battery room.

Frequency: Annually, during the planned outage in the first quarter.

Procedure:

1. De-energise the busbar section and apply lockout/tagout.
2. Verify the absence of voltage at the work location.
3. Using a calibrated torque wrench, check each bolted connection
   against the torque values in the table below.
4. Re-torque any connection found below the minimum value.
5. Mark the connection with a torque seal and record the reading in
   the maintenance log.

| Connection Size | Torque (N·m) |
|-----------------|--------------|
| M8              | 20-24        |
| M10             | 35-42        |
| M12             | 60-72        |

This procedure was introduced in 2019 following a thermal imaging
survey that identified two loose connections. It is current.

documents.content:
**4.2.6 Inverter Cooling Fan Bearing Replacement (Procedure MP-412)**

Applicable equipment: Inverter units INV-01 through INV-06 (ABB PVS-800, 500 kW each) and INV-07/INV-08 (SMA Sunny Central, 630 kW each).

Frequency: Every 24 months or at 20,000 operating hours, whichever comes first. The hour counter for each inverter is recorded in the CMMS and is also displayed on the local HMI.

Procedure:

1. Isolate the inverter at the AC and DC sides and apply lockout/tagout.
2. Allow the inverter to cool for a minimum of 30 minutes before opening the cabinet.
3. Remove the fan guard and the fan assembly. Note the orientation of the fan before removal.
4. Inspect the fan housing for cracks or distortion. If the housing is damaged, replace the complete fan assembly.
5. Install the new bearing, packing it with the supplied lithium-based grease. Do not over-pack.
6. Refit the fan assembly and guard, and restore power.
7. Run the inverter in test mode for 15 minutes and confirm the fan speed and the absence of abnormal vibration or noise. Record the bearing replacement date and the hour counter reading in the maintenance log.

Spare parts are held in the main store under the following codes:
- Fan assembly ABB: SP-FAN-ABB-01
- Fan assembly SMA: SP-FAN-SMA-02
- Bearing kit (fits both): SP-BRG-KIT-01

This procedure was revised in March 2022 to include the 20,000-hour trigger. The previous revision (2018) specified a fixed 24-month interval only. The revision was prompted by two premature bearing failures on INV-03 that were traced to dust ingress; the hour-based trigger ensures replacement before the duty cycle becomes excessive in dusty periods.

**4.2.7 Combiner Box Inspection and I-V Curve Tracing (Procedure MP-505)**

Applicable equipment: All DC combiner boxes (CB-01 through CB-48) feeding the inverter halls.

Frequency: Quarterly, during the first full week of the quarter. Additional I-V curve tracing is performed on any string that shows a current deviation greater than 5% from its sister strings during the routine inspection.

Procedure:

1. Visually inspect the combiner box enclosure for signs of water ingress, corrosion, or animal activity.
2. Check that all DC fuse indicators are in the normal (not blown) position.
3. Using the PV analyzer, perform an I-V curve trace on each string. Compare the curve to the baseline curve stored in the analyzer for that string.
4. Flag any string where the measured maximum power point (MPP) is more than 8% below the baseline MPP.
5. For flagged strings, check the module connections and the bypass diodes. If no fault is found, schedule a thermal imaging scan of the string.
6. Record the trace data and the inspection results in the CMMS.

The baseline curves were last updated in February 2024 after the module cleaning campaign. Any string not traced in the previous quarter must be prioritised in the current quarter.

**4.2.8 Oil Leak Inspection on Pad-Mounted Transformers (Procedure MP-601)**

Applicable equipment: Pad-mounted transformers TX-01 through TX-04 (1,000 kVA, 11/0.415 kV) serving the auxiliary loads.

Frequency: Monthly, on the first Monday of the month.

Procedure:

1. Walk around the transformer and inspect the base for oil stains or puddles.
2. Check the breather for silica gel colour change. The gel must be blue; if it is pink or white, replace the breather.
3. Inspect the radiators and welds for seepage. Use a torch in low light.
4. Check the oil level gauge. The level must be within the marked operating band.
5. If a leak is found, estimate the leak rate and report it to the Shift Charge Engineer. A leak rate of more than one drop per minute requires a work order to be raised for repair. A small seepage may be monitored and recorded in the log.

**KANO HYBRID POWER STATION**
**Engineering Records – Maintenance Procedures Manual (Volume 2)**

**Document Ref:** KHP/ENG/MP/02

**Effective Date:** 10 March 2025
**Prepared By:** A. Bello, Senior Maintenance Engineer
**Approved By:** C. Okafor, Plant Manager

**4.3.1 General Lubrication Schedule (Procedure MP-701)**

Applicable equipment: All rotating machinery within the power block, including but not limited to diesel generator sets DG-01 through DG-04 (Caterpillar 3516, 1,250 kVA each), the cooling water pump motors P-01 through P-06, and the ventilation fan motors VF-01 through VF-08.

Frequency: As per the equipment manufacturer's recommendations, and in any case not exceeding the intervals listed in Table 4.3.1-1 below.

**Table 4.3.1-1: Lubrication Intervals**

| Equipment Group | Lubricant Type | Interval | Remarks |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| DG-01 through DG-04 – Engine Crankcase | SAE 15W-40 (API CJ-4) | 250 hours | Oil sample to be drawn for analysis at every change. |
| DG-01 through DG-04 – Generator Bearings | NLGI Grade 2 Grease | 500 hours | Check for grease purge from the relief valve. |
| P-01 through P-06 – Pump Bearings | NLGI Grade 2 Grease | 1,000 hours | Do not over-grease. |
| VF-01 through VF-08 – Motor Bearings | NLGI Grade 2 Grease | 2,000 hours | |

Procedure:

1.  Ensure the equipment is isolated and locked out before commencing any lubrication work.
2.  Clean the grease fittings and surrounding area with a lint-free cloth before applying new grease.
3.  Use only the specified lubricant. If a substitute is required, it must be approved by the Shift Charge Engineer and recorded in the CMMS.
4.  Record the date, the equipment tag number, the quantity of lubricant used, and the technician's initials in the CMMS work order.
5.  Any abnormal noise, heat, or vibration noticed during the lubrication round must be reported immediately to the Shift Charge Engineer.

A recurring issue has been over-greasing of the pump bearings, which leads to premature bearing failure. The quantity of grease per application is limited to two pumps of the grease gun for small bearings and five pumps for large bearings.

**4.3.2 Cooling Water System – Chemical Dosing and Testing (Procedure MP-702)**

Applicable equipment: Cooling water system serving DG-01 through DG-04, including the cooling towers CT-01 and CT-02 and the associated piping.

Frequency: Daily, at 09:00 hours.

Procedure:

1.  Collect a water sample from the sample point on the main return header.
2.  Test for pH, conductivity, and chloride concentration using the portable test kit.
3.  Record the results in the daily log sheet (Form KHP/LOG/COOL-01).
4.  If the pH is outside the range of 8.0 to 9.0, adjust by adding the appropriate chemical from the dosing skid.
5.  If the conductivity exceeds 3,000 µS/cm, increase the bleed rate to the drain.
6.  If the chloride concentration exceeds 200 ppm, report to the Shift Charge Engineer. This may indicate a leak from the heat exchangers or contamination from the raw water source.
7.  The chemical dosing pump levels are to be checked daily. If the level in any drum is below 20%, a new drum must be staged and the empty one removed.

**4.3.3 Fire Suppression System – Weekly Check (Procedure MP-703)**

Applicable equipment: The fixed CO2 fire suppression system protecting the DG hall and the electrical rooms, and the portable fire extinguishers located throughout the plant.

**5. Warranty Terms and Conditions**

**5.1 Standard Warranty Coverage**

The Alpha Solar Array inverter is covered by a standard manufacturer warranty of 5 years
from the date of commissioning. This warranty covers defects in materials and workmanship
under normal use and service conditions. The warranty does not cover:

- Damage caused by improper installation, operation, or maintenance
- Damage caused by external factors, including lightning, flooding, fire, or vandalism
- Damage caused by unauthorized modification or repair
- Normal wear and tear, including cosmetic degradation
- Damage caused by operation outside the specified environmental limits

The warranty is transferable to a subsequent owner of the system, provided that the
original installation records are available and the system has been serviced in accordance
with the maintenance recommendations in Section 6.

**5.2 Extended Warranty Options**

An extended warranty of an additional 5 years (total 10 years) is available for purchase
at the time of installation or within the first 12 months of operation. The extended
warranty covers the same items as the standard warranty. The cost of the extended
warranty is based on the inverter model and the site location. For the Alpha Solar Array
site in Nigeria, the extended warranty is priced at 8% of the inverter purchase price.

**5.3 Warranty Exclusions for Environmental Conditions**

The standard warranty does not cover damage caused by operation at ambient temperatures
above 55°C or below -10°C. As noted in Section 4.5, the inverter may shut down if internal
temperatures exceed 85°C. Operation in such conditions may void the warranty. Sites in
tropical climates should ensure adequate ventilation and shading of the inverter to
maintain operating temperatures within the specified range.

**5.4 Warranty Claim Procedure**

To file a warranty claim, the following information must be provided:

- Inverter model and serial number
- Date of commissioning
- Installation records, including electrical diagrams
- Maintenance records, including any cleaning or service logs
- Description of the fault and any error codes displayed

Claims must be submitted through the authorized distributor or installer. The manufacturer
will respond within 14 business days of receiving a complete claim. If the claim is
approved, the manufacturer will provide a replacement unit or repair service. Shipping
costs for the replacement unit are covered by the manufacturer for the first 2 years of
the warranty period. After 2 years, the customer is responsible for shipping costs.

**5.5 Warranty Status for the Alpha Solar Array**

The Alpha Solar Array inverter was commissioned in March 2017. The standard 5-year
warranty is current and will expire in March 2022. The extended warranty option was not
purchased at the time of installation. The system owner has the option to purchase the
extended warranty until March 2018, which would extend coverage to March 2027.
